title: Kedoshim: no stumbling block (Leviticus 19:14)
hook: don't put a stumbling block before the blind; the rabbis read it as never misleading anyone

segments.voice: Yesterday in Kedoshim, pe'ah, the corners of the field. Your line was leave the corners. Today, a verse that starts literal and keeps growing.

A friend is about to buy a used car, and asks what you think. You happen to know the transmission is shot. You also happen to want that car yourself, and if they pass, the price will drop. So you say, eh, I'd look at other options. Nobody would ever know why you said it. Nothing you said was even false. Leviticus 19 has a short verse about a blind man and an obstacle in the road. The rabbis read it, and found your friend and the car inside it.
screen: `A FRIEND ASKS ABOUT A CAR.` → `NOBODY WOULD EVER KNOW.` → `A BLIND MAN AND A ROAD.`

segments.voice: The verse, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "Thou shalt not curse the deaf, nor put a stumbling-block before the blind, but thou shalt fear thy God: I am the LORD." Plainly, it means what it says. Don't trip someone who can't see it coming. Don't curse someone who can't hear it. Then the widening. The Sifra, an early rabbinic commentary on Leviticus, reads the blind as anyone blind in a matter, anyone who can't see what you can see. If someone asks your advice, don't give advice that isn't good for them. Its example: don't say sell your field and buy a donkey, when you're secretly planning to buy that field yourself. The Talmud stretches it further: don't hand a cup of wine to someone who has vowed not to drink. Don't help another person do the wrong they're already reaching for. A stumbling block can be an offer, a nudge, a door held open. And why does the verse close with fear thy God? Rashi answers: because nobody else can check. Only you know whether your advice was honest or self-serving. That's exactly what makes the other person blind in this matter, and why the verse hands the case to God. Today the principle is cited in Jewish discussions of business ethics, financial advice and selling to people who can't judge what they're buying.
screen: `DON'T TRIP THE ONE WHO CAN'T SEE.` · `BLIND IN A MATTER.` · `NO CUP FOR THE ONE WHO VOWED.` · `ONLY YOU KNOW YOUR INTENT.` · then, large: `NO STUMBLING BLOCKS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who has asked your opinion lately, or is about to: about a job, a purchase, a relationship. Ask yourself honestly whether you'd gain anything from what you tell them, or are tempted to leave something out. Then picture giving the advice you'd want in their place, even if it costs you something.
Kedoshim. The portion that forbids a stumbling block before the blind, which the rabbis read as never misleading anyone who can't see what you see.
Your line: no stumbling blocks. Only you can see behind your own advice. Day four hundred twelve, done.

howItsDone: Jewish law applies lifnei iver, the stumbling-block principle, to advice, business dealings and helping others do wrong, and it appears in rabbinic rulings on everything from selling dangerous goods to giving biased counsel.

chat.says: If I never actually lie, is it fine to steer a friend's choice toward what helps me?
options: No; the rabbis read it as misleading anyone who can't see what you see.
Yes; the verse only forbids tripping people who are physically blind.
Yes; as long as no words are false, the advice counts as honest.
